en_US.LOC_META_100_BODY: Similar to the Technology Tree, the Civics Tree has different choices and paths as you progress through the game.[NEWLINE]For this tutorial, click the Craftsmanship civic to start advancing next.
en_US.LOC_META_100c_BODY: Click to close the Civics Tree
en_US.LOC_META_102_BODY: Click Builder to begin training a Builder unit.
en_US.LOC_META_103_BODY: The city is the cornerstone of any great civilization. A city’s size is represented by its [ICON_Citizen] Population, indicated to the left of its nameplate.
en_US.LOC_META_103_OTHER_BODY: A Slinger unit has finished training in your capital. Slingers are ranged class units, allowing them to attack from distance without engaging in melee combat. This keeps them from taking reciprocal damage during the attack.
en_US.LOC_META_104_BODY: Each city also claims the surrounding lands for your exclusive control. These lands are indicated by the colored border surrounding the city. The unique features within your borders will have a profound influence on the potential strengths of each city.
en_US.LOC_META_104_OTHER_BODY: Ranged units also tend to have lower defense strength than their melee fighting counterparts, so it is best to keep them close to friendly units of other types for protection.
en_US.LOC_META_105_BODY: You must choose how each city in your civilization is to grow and expand over time, improving the land you control and creating new buildings and districts within your borders.
en_US.LOC_META_105_OTHER_BODY: As you progress through the game and research new technologies, you will unlock better, stronger, and more advanced units. Building a strong and diverse fighting force is essential in competing against other civilizations, and preserving the safety of your people.
en_US.LOC_META_106_BODY: Each city generates a variety of yields at the start of every turn. These are obtained from the hexes that the city controls.
en_US.LOC_META_107_BODY: Each hex within your city borders can provide a number of yields to help you advance your civilization. [ICON_Food] Food and [ICON_Production] Production are two of these yields.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE] [ICON_Food] Food fuels city growth, increasing its [ICON_Citizen] Population. More [ICON_Food] Food, faster growth.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]  [ICON_Production] Production is used to build new items, like military units and city upgrades. The more [ICON_Production] Production your city has, the faster you can build things.
en_US.LOC_META_108_BODY: However, each hex will need to be worked by your [ICON_Citizen] Population in order to obtain the yield from that hex.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]Each [ICON_Citizen] Citizen can work 1 hex within your borders.
en_US.LOC_META_109_BODY: Growing your city’s [ICON_Citizen] Population is very important in order to take advantage of all the yields from the surrounding lands.
en_US.LOC_META_10_BODY: Military units can attack enemy units by moving into their hex. Right-click on the Barbarian unit to attack it. Try doing that now.
en_US.LOC_META_110_BODY: It is now up to you to decide what you would like to produce in this city.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]Suggestions:[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]- Train a Builder to improve more of the surrounding lands within your borders.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]- Train a combat unit to expand the size and strength of your military.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]-Build a Granary to provide additional [ICON_Food] Food for your city as well as more [ICON_Housing] Housing for your [ICON_Citizen] Population.
en_US.LOC_META_111_BODY: Just as building new units is fueled by [ICON_Production] Production, researching new technologies is fueled by [ICON_Science] Science.
en_US.LOC_META_112_BODY: Each city in your empire generates a small amount of [ICON_Science] Science per turn. How quickly your research projects are completed is determined by the total of all the [ICON_Science] Science generated by your cities. [NEWLINE][NEWLINE]The more [ICON_Science] Science you generate, the faster you research new technologies.
en_US.LOC_META_113_BODY: For the purposes of this tutorial, we have ‘rushed’ the production of this unit. Normally, the production would have taken several more turns to complete.
en_US.LOC_META_114_BODY: All Tribal Villages will grant a reward when explored by a player. This Tribal Village has granted you a new Scout unit, which has appeared in your city.
en_US.LOC_META_115_BODY: Continue exploring the world with your Scout. End turn when its action is complete.
en_US.LOC_META_116_BODY: Your civilization will always be researching a technology. Because you just completed Mining, you must now choose what to research next before you can progress to the next turn.
en_US.LOC_META_117_BODY: Research has begun on the Pottery technology. End your turn once you have moved your Scout unit.
en_US.LOC_META_118_BODY: To win a game of Civilization, you need to defeat all other civilizations in the world. There are multiple ways to achieve this. Most games will also end in the year 2050 or after a set number of turns. If no player has achieved these Victories by then, score will determine the winner. Score is calculated as a general measure of each player’s achievements in all fields of endeavor.
en_US.LOC_META_119_BODY: The status of each Victory’s conditions are tracked on the World Rankings panel. [NEWLINE][NEWLINE]Open it now.
en_US.LOC_META_119a_BODY: Click to open the World Rankings panel
en_US.LOC_META_11_BODY: Click the Choose Production notification to select your next production task.
en_US.LOC_META_11a_BODY: Tasks which must be completed before you can end your turn will appear in the notification panel in the bottom right of the screen.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]Since production has finished in this city, you get a reminder that you need to choose the next thing to produce before you can end your turn.
en_US.LOC_META_120_BODY: The Overall tab gives you an overview of all types of Victory and your ranking against other players
en_US.LOC_META_121_BODY: The other tabs give you more specific detail about each set of rankings. [NEWLINE][NEWLINE]Close the panel when you are ready to proceed.
en_US.LOC_META_122_BODY: The rest of this tutorial will help you to achieve your first Domination Victory.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]The goal of a Domination Victory is for your civilization to be the last to occupy its own [ICON_Capital] Capital city.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]For this tutorial, that means you will have to use your military to capture the [ICON_Capital] Capital city of your rival, while preventing them from taking yours.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]How you ultimately achieve this will be up to you. However, we have provided three optional objectives that, if completed, will greatly assist you in achieving this.
en_US.LOC_META_123_BODY: If you are unsure about something, or are looking for more information about anything you’ve seen in this tutorial, there’s a good chance you’ll find it in the Civilopedia.
en_US.LOC_META_124_BODY: In developing your military, it is always a good strategy to diversify. Not all units are created equal, some are better against others, and have abilities that separate them from the rest.
en_US.LOC_META_125_BODY: The [ICON_Citizen] Population of your first city has grown from 1 to 2. As long as a city is well fed and its people are happy, it will continue to grow. The [ICON_Citizen] Citizens of the city work the surrounding plots and improvements contributing to greater yields. Higher [ICON_Citizen] Populations contribute to faster [ICON_Science] Science research, faster city [ICON_Production] Production, and faster [ICON_Culture] Cultural growth.
en_US.LOC_META_126_BODY: It is always a good strategy to not only found new cities to expand your realm, but also to grow those cities.
en_US.LOC_META_127_BODY: Scouts are ideal for investigating Tribal Villages because they receive experience from it.
en_US.LOC_META_128_BODY: You may have noticed that your cities have been generating a small amount of [ICON_Faith] Faith each turn.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE][ICON_Faith] Faith is earned over time by certain buildings, districts, and policies.
en_US.LOC_META_129_BODY: Now that you’ve earned enough [ICON_Faith] Faith, you are able to take the first step towards founding a Religion by forming a Pantheon, which will provide you with a choice of strategic benefits.
en_US.LOC_META_129b_BODY: Click the Religion button to open the Religion screen and choose a Pantheon.
en_US.LOC_META_129c: There are many Pantheons to choose from with different gameplay effects. Once one is chosen by a player, it is removed from the list of available Pantheons and is exclusive to that player’s religion for the duration of the game. Choose wisely!
en_US.LOC_META_129d: Choose a Pantheon, then click the 'Found this Pantheon' button when you are done.
en_US.LOC_META_12_BODY: Click the Choose Production notification to open the city’s Production Menu.
en_US.LOC_META_130_BODY: Well done! The next step is to attract a Great Prophet, who will be able to found a Religion. But first, you will need to build a Holy Site district, or enact an appropriate government policy, both of which will earn you Great Prophet Points.
en_US.LOC_META_131_BODY: There are a limited number of opportunities to found a Religion. Doing so is optional, but keep in mind that if you do not, you may not have an effective counter against a player who is seeking a Religious Victory by converting your [ICON_Citizen] Citizens.
en_US.LOC_META_132_BODY: Your [ICON_GreatProphet] Great Prophet has founded a new Religion, and you must customize it by selecting a name, symbol, and selecting two additional religious beliefs that will complement the Pantheon belief you selected previously.
en_US.LOC_META_133_BODY: Your new Religion can spread between cities, converting its [ICON_Citizen] Citizens into followers. It is possible for a city to have a mix of several Religions. The Religion with the majority of followers in a city will be the one that imparts its bonuses.
en_US.LOC_META_134_BODY: While Religion will slowly spread from city to city organically, you can cause sudden shifts by training Missionary and Apostle units and sending them out to spread your people’s Religion. These units can be obtained by spending [ICON_Faith] Faith to buy them in the Purchase tab of a city’s Production Menu.
en_US.LOC_META_135_BODY: Aggressively spreading your Religion is essential if you are targeting a Religious Victory. Even if you are not, it is wise to keep track of how Religion is spreading around the world. Counter it where possible to mitigate the chances of another player claiming Victory this way.
en_US.LOC_META_136_BODY: You have gained the opportunity to claim a [ICON_GreatPerson] Great Person for your civilization. [ICON_GreatPerson] Great People provide significant benefits to your civilization based on their field. There are many types of [ICON_GreatPerson] Great People, including artists, engineers, and military leaders.
en_US.LOC_META_136b_BODY: Open the [ICON_GreatPerson] Great People panel to claim your [ICON_GreatPerson] Great Person.
en_US.LOC_META_137_BODY: This is the [ICON_GreatPerson] Great People panel. It shows all the [ICON_GreatPerson] Great People that are currently available for civilizations to claim, their benefits, and their costs.
en_US.LOC_META_138_BODY: Each [ICON_GreatPerson] Great Person has one or more opportunities to activate a special bonus. They will appear as a unit in one of your cities and you must Activate their bonus at a special location on the map. Once they have used all their bonuses, the [ICON_GreatPerson] Great Person will disappear.
en_US.LOC_META_139_BODY: A [ICON_GreatPerson] Great Person is earned by saving up enough [ICON_GreatPerson] Great People Points of its type, then spending them to recruit the [ICON_GreatPerson] Great Person to your civilization. These points come primarily from districts and buildings, but can also come from policies and other effects. If you are in a rush, you can spend [ICON_Gold] Gold or [ICON_Faith] Faith to instantly earn the [ICON_GreatPerson] Great Person you want.
en_US.LOC_META_13_BODY: Click the Next Turn button to continue.
en_US.LOC_META_13a_BODY: A Builder unit has been added to the city's Production Queue. It will take several turns to complete its training. Since there are no remaining decisions that need to be made this turn, the Next Turn button is displayed.
en_US.LOC_META_140_BODY: You can choose to pass on a [ICON_GreatPerson] Great Person that you don’t want. If you do this, then other players will have the opportunity to claim them, and your choice to pass is not reversible. However, your [ICON_GreatPerson] Great People Points will be saved for a future opportunity.
en_US.LOC_META_141_BODY: You’ve just completed a Trader unit. Traders travel between two cities and generate income for their city of origin.
en_US.LOC_META_142_BODY: Your civilization can establish a limited number of [ICON_TradeRoute] Trade Routes. You can expand this capacity with Commercial Hub or Harbor districts.
en_US.LOC_META_142b_BODY: Click the 'Assign Trade Route' unit action.
en_US.LOC_META_143_BODY: There are no other cities to trade with right now. Continue to explore the map, or build a Settler and found a new city of your own.
en_US.LOC_META_144_BODY: This is the Trade Panel, showing the cities that you can trade with currently. Traders have a limited range, but visiting nearby cities will establish a Trading Post there, allowing them to be used as a bridge to farther destinations.
en_US.LOC_META_145_BODY: Depending on the buildings and districts within a foreign destination, you stand to earn yields of [ICON_Science] Science, [ICON_Faith] Faith, [ICON_Culture] Culture, or [ICON_Gold] Gold each turn for a set number of turns. For domestic destinations, you can earn [ICON_Food] Food and [ICON_Production] Production.
en_US.LOC_META_145b_BODY: Select the destination of your choice from the list of available cities.
en_US.LOC_META_145c_BODY: Click 'Begin Route' to send this Trader on its way to the destination.
en_US.LOC_META_146_BODY: This Trader will now travel to the destination and back, generating the relevant yields each turn. Once it has returned, you can choose a new route.
en_US.LOC_META_147_BODY: The Trader will also build a Road between the cities as it goes. Units travelling a road generally suffer no terrain [ICON_Movement] Movement penalties.
en_US.LOC_META_148_BODY: You have discovered a nearby city-state. These are mini-civilizations that are similar in some ways to another player, but they can only ever have a single city and cannot win the game. By working with your city-state neighbors, you can build lucrative relationships and even gain their support in war.
en_US.LOC_META_149_BODY: You can also choose to forcefully assimilate their cities into your empire or raze them to the ground – but they are far more formidable than Barbarians to defeat, and you risk alienating their other allies.
en_US.LOC_META_14_BODY: At the beginning of the game, your city and the lands immediately around it are revealed, but the areas beyond, represented by blank parchment, indicate parts of the world you have not yet explored.
en_US.LOC_META_150_BODY: Click the city-state button or click the city-state to open the city state panel.
en_US.LOC_META_151_BODY: This is the city-state panel. You can earn Envoys and dispatch them to a city-state. Doing this can earn you progressively better buffs to [ICON_Science] Science, [ICON_Culture] Culture, [ICON_Production] Production, [ICON_Gold] Gold, or [ICON_Faith] Faith. Click the name of a city-state in the list.
en_US.LOC_META_152_BODY: These are the Quests you can complete for this city-state. This is one way to earn Envoys and improve your friendship with it. You can also earn Envoys by completing certain items in the Civics Tree, and over time through governments and policies.
en_US.LOC_META_153_BODY: Your unit is getting close to an enemy city. Attacking cities is usually a difficult and potentially costly undertaking that requires a mix of unit types and a tactical approach.
en_US.LOC_META_154_BODY: The city’s defense rating and health bar is shown on its Name Plate. This city has Walls. It will be able to launch a ranged attack from 2 hexes away, and will be highly resistant to melee units.
en_US.LOC_META_155_BODY: Certain siege units can improve your chances. Catapults can attack from range and do significant damage to Walls, while the Battering Ram or Siege Tower allows melee units to attack Walls or bypass them, respectively.
en_US.LOC_META_156_BODY: You have met the leader of another civilization. In Civilization VI, there will typically be several other civilizations sharing the world map with you. These are controlled by the game AI, and have all the same abilities – and ambitions – that you do.
en_US.LOC_META_157_BODY: As you play, you will need to consider how to deal with your neighbors and watch them carefully to improve your understanding of their strategy.
en_US.LOC_META_158_BODY: Leaders of civilizations you have met in the game will appear here. The leader icon on the far right represents your civilization. All other leaders will be listed to next to yours.
en_US.LOC_META_158b_BODY: Click the other civilization leader's icon to access the Diplomacy view.
en_US.LOC_META_159_BODY: When you contact another leader, you can take a variety of actions, like exchanging goods, negotiating political treaties, making demands, or declaring war.
en_US.LOC_META_15_BODY: Click on the Warrior unit to select it.
en_US.LOC_META_160_BODY: You can send a Delegation to improve your ties and expose more information about their [ICON_Capital] Capital city.
en_US.LOC_META_161_BODY: Denouncing a rival notifies all other civilizations that you have a bone to pick. This paves the way to war. If you do not make your feelings known, the war you declare will be a Surprise War, inflicting a lasting “Warmonger” reputation on you that may color future dealings with other leaders.
en_US.LOC_META_162_BODY: You can also negotiate deals with a leader. This can include trading commodities or political deals like Open Borders or Joint War. Alternatively, you can demand that they deal with you. This will sour your relationship, but they may acquiesce if they are weak or wish to avoid war.
en_US.LOC_META_163_BODY: What you know about this leader is summarized here. Be mindful of their Agendas. If you act in opposition to their Agendas, your relationship with them may sour and potentially lead to conflict.
en_US.LOC_META_164_BODY: Improving your Access Level to this civilization will expose more detailed information about them, and you’ll be notified when they take certain actions. It's a good idea to improve this as much as possible with the leaders you encounter, or you will be in the dark as to their strategy.
en_US.LOC_META_165_BODY: This section explains what the leader thinks about you, and why. If you wish to improve (or sour) your relationship, you’ll find some suggestions here. It may not be possible to avoid doing something that annoys them from time to time, so it can be useful to know how to balance the books.
en_US.LOC_META_166_BODY: Diplomacy will become increasingly important as you progress through history. Who your neighbors are and want they want will have a lasting impact on the development of your civilization – and will almost certainly present obstacles in your path to victory.
en_US.LOC_META_167_BODY: The technological advancement of your people is attained through research.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]By completing research on technologies you will unlock new ways to exploit the land, new military units, new city upgrades, and much more.
en_US.LOC_META_168_BODY: A City-State is a small civilization that cannot win the game. Establishing good diplomatic relations with them can be very lucrative. This is done by sending Envoys to the City State.
en_US.LOC_META_169_BODY: Trader units can be trained in one of your cities. In addition to providing additional [ICON_Gold] Gold and other benefits to your civilization, [ICON_TradeRoute] Trade Routes are essential for building roads between cities.
en_US.LOC_META_16_BODY: Warrior units have a [ICON_Movement] Movement range of 2.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]The blue colored indicator shown on the lands around the unit displays the furthest the selected unit can move in a single turn.
en_US.LOC_META_17_BODY: Open terrain, like Plains and Grassland, only consume 1 [ICON_Movement] Movement point, whereas more difficult terrain, like Woods and Hills, will consume 2 or more [ICON_Movement] Movement points. Move the Warrior unit to the highlighted location by right clicking.
en_US.LOC_META_17b_BODY: RIGHT-CLICK the highlighted location to move your Warrior.
en_US.LOC_META_18_BODY: Exploring Tribal Villages can give your civilization one of many instant benefits, like granting an additional [ICON_Citizen] Population in your city, or awarding [ICON_Gold] Gold. It is a good strategy to explore as many Tribal Villages as possible.
en_US.LOC_META_19_BODY: Since your Warrior unit has used all of its [ICON_Movement] Movement points, it is done with its actions this turn.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]Production and research tasks are still in progress, so there are no other decisions to be made.
en_US.LOC_META_19b_BODY: Click the Next Turn button once again to continue.
en_US.LOC_META_1_BODY: Click on the Settler unit to select it.
en_US.LOC_META_20_BODY: To explore a Tribal Village, move one of your units into the Tribal Village hex. Try moving your Warrior unit there now.
en_US.LOC_META_21_BODY: Notice that the Scout unit has a [ICON_Movement] Movement of 3, allowing it to move a greater distance than other units. Move the Scout unit toward an undiscovered part of the map.
en_US.LOC_META_22_BODY: Builders can construct a wide variety of improvements to your land. The type of improvement they can build on a plot is often determined by the type of terrain. Plains and Grassland plots are ideal for Farms, which help increase [ICON_Citizen] Population.
en_US.LOC_META_23_BODY: Move your Builder to the highlighted Plains area next to your city.
en_US.LOC_META_24_BODY: Construct a Farm improvement here by clicking on the "Build Improvement: Farm" button next to the Unit Panel.
en_US.LOC_META_25_BODY: Constructing a Farm here has increased the [ICON_Food] Food yield from this plot from 1 [ICON_Food] Food per turn to 2. The amount of [ICON_Food] Food generated by your city determines how fast the Population of that city grows, granting you new [ICON_Citizen] Citizens to work more tiles. More [ICON_Food] Food means faster growth.
en_US.LOC_META_26_BODY: Builders can build up to 3 improvements before exhausting their workforce. This number is indicated in the Unit Panel. This Builder unit has consumed one of its workforce from building the Farm and now has 2 remaining.
en_US.LOC_META_27_BODY: In addition to training units, your city can focus its production on constructing buildings like the Monument.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]Try building one now by selecting it in the city's Production Queue.
en_US.LOC_META_28_BODY: Try ordering the Warrior to return to the city by clicking the Move To button, then clicking the city.
en_US.LOC_META_28a_BODY: Units can be ordered to move longer distances by giving them a multi-turn order. This will eliminate the need to give a separate move order every turn to reach a destination.
en_US.LOC_META_29_BODY: When using a multi-move order, a path will display on the map indicating the path the unit will take, along with indicators of the number of turns until it reaches the destination.
en_US.LOC_META_2_BODY: Click the Found City button to order your Settler to found a new city at this location.
en_US.LOC_META_30_BODY: Scattered around the map are resources of various kinds. There are 3 categories of resources:[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]Luxury: These contribute to the overall happiness of your citizens.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]Strategic: Essential for creating some very powerful military units.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]Bonus: Provide additional yields of [ICON_Food] Food , [ICON_Production] Production, or [ICON_Gold] Gold.
en_US.LOC_META_31a_BODY: This Stone is a Bonus resource. It provides an additional +1 [ICON_Production]Production to your city.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]If you build a Quarry improvement here, it will raise the yield to +2 [ICON_Production]Production.
en_US.LOC_META_31b_BODY: Move your Builder unit to the Stone resource and have them construct a Quarry improvement there.
en_US.LOC_META_32_BODY: Quarry improvements increase the [ICON_Production]Production of the city they're in. Higher Production allows units and buildings to be constructed faster. In short, the higher the Production of a city, the less turns required to build something there.
en_US.LOC_META_332_BODY: Click the Choose Research button to display the research chooser.
en_US.LOC_META_33_BODY: Select the Pottery technology from the Research Menu.
en_US.LOC_META_33b_BODY: Research must be selected before the turn can be completed.
en_US.LOC_META_34_BODY: If there are units that have not moved this turn and are awaiting orders, you can address them by clicking the Unit Needs Orders notification. Click the notification now to be taken to your Scout unit so you may issue new orders.
en_US.LOC_META_35_BODY: Continue to explore the world with your Scout unit.
en_US.LOC_META_36_BODY: Try ordering the Warrior unit to do so by clicking on the Fortify button.
en_US.LOC_META_36a_BODY: When not advancing a military unit, it is often a good idea to fortify the unit. When ordered to fortify, the unit will spend up to 2 turns digging in. This will increase their [ICON_Strength] Combat Strength if they are attacked.
en_US.LOC_META_37_BODY: This unit will now have an advantage in combat when defending. However, if the unit is moved it will lose its fortified status and will have to be ordered to fortify again in order to receive the bonus.
en_US.LOC_META_38a_BODY: Your Builder still has one of its workforce remaining.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]You can use it to build either a Mine on the Hill plot (+[ICON_Production] Production), or a Farm on the Plains plot (+[ICON_Food] Food).[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]This may take more than one turn, one to move the Builder unit, and another turn to build the improvement.
en_US.LOC_META_38b_BODY: Remember: Builders can only construct improvements within the borders of your city.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]By generating [ICON_Culture] Culture, the borders of your city will expand, allowing you access to more resources.
en_US.LOC_META_39_BODY: Feel free to continue exploring the map with your Scout unit. End your turn when you have finished giving orders to your Builder and Scout.
en_US.LOC_META_3_BODY: Open the Production Chooser of this city by clicking the Change City Production button.
en_US.LOC_META_40_BODY: Your city has finished production on the Monument building. All buildings contribute to a city’s development in specific ways. The Monument will increase the [ICON_Culture] Culture generated by the city, which extends the city’s influence over additional hexes.
en_US.LOC_META_41b_BODY: Open the Production Chooser and begin training a Settler unit. Remember, the Production Chooser can either be accessed from the city's Information Panel or from the Choose Production reminder in the Notification Panel on the right side of the game view.
en_US.LOC_META_42_BODY: Units like Settlers and Builders are non-combat, civilian units and thus cannot defend themselves. This leaves them highly vulnerable to be captured or killed by enemy units. However, your military units can act as protection for the civilian unit if they occupy the same hex.
en_US.LOC_META_43_BODY: Select either the Settler or the Warrior and click the Escort button in the unit panel.
en_US.LOC_META_43a_BODY: An easy way to move the two units together is by linking them together until they reach their destination.
en_US.LOC_META_44_BODY: Begin moving the units southeast toward the indicated map marker. If you have not yet revealed that part of the map it might make your journey easier if you sent your Scout there as well.
en_US.LOC_META_45_BODY: Add a Slinger unit to the city's Production Queue and end your turn when you are finished.
en_US.LOC_META_45a_BODY: In a game of Civilization, once a player loses all of their cities, the game is over. It is very important that you protect your cities, especially your [ICON_Capital] Capital, from any foreign threat.
en_US.LOC_META_46_BODY: As is often the case in history, technological discoveries inspire new technologies, building upon knowledge gained in the past. In a game of Civilization, this is simulated by the Technology Tree. Click the open Technology Tree button in the Research Panel to view it.
en_US.LOC_META_46a_BODY: Click to open the Technology Tree
en_US.LOC_META_47_BODY: The Technology Tree displays all of the researchable technologies available in a game of Civilization, from the Ancient era all the way to the Information era and beyond.
en_US.LOC_META_48_BODY: The gold colored nodes represent technologies that you have already finished researching. You have just finished researching Pottery, so it has been marked as complete.
en_US.LOC_META_49_BODY: The dark grey nodes represent technologies that are available to begin researching, but are not complete.
en_US.LOC_META_4a_BODY: This is the city's Production Chooser. From here you can construct buildings, create wonders of the world, and train military and civilian units.
en_US.LOC_META_4b_BODY: Select the Warrior button to start training a Warrior unit in your city.
en_US.LOC_META_50_BODY: Light grey nodes represent technologies that are not yet available to begin researching. These technologies need to first be unlocked by researching one or more prerequisite technologies.
en_US.LOC_META_51_BODY: Start research on Writing by clicking on the Writing node in the Technology Tree.
en_US.LOC_META_51a_BODY: Since we have already researched Pottery, we are now able to begin research on the Writing technology.
en_US.LOC_META_52_BODY: Notice the Writing technology node status has changed, indicating that it is currently being researched. The number of turns required to finish research on a technology is indicated in the upper right corner of the node.
en_US.LOC_META_53A_BODY: The symbols displayed inside the technology node represent new units, buildings, wonders and abilities that are unlocked by the technology once it is completed.
en_US.LOC_META_53B_BODY: For example, once you have finished researching the Writing technology, you will be able to construct the Campus district as well as the Library building in all of your cities. The Campus and Library allow you to increase the amount of [ICON_Science] Science you generate each turn, allowing you to research technologies faster!
en_US.LOC_META_53_BODY: The symbols displayed inside the technology node represent new units, buildings, wonders, and abilities that are unlocked by the technology once it is completed. For example, once you have finished researching the Pottery technology, you will be able to construct the Granary building in all of your cities. Your Builders will also gain the ability to harvest Wheat resources near your city. While harvesting a Wheat resource gives you a large amount of [ICON_Food] Food, that resource is removed from the map. In most cases, it is better to nurture a Wheat resource by building a Farm improvement on it instead.
en_US.LOC_META_54_BODY: Since you're done designating new research, we can close the Technology Tree by clicking the X button in the upper right corner.
en_US.LOC_META_54a_BODY: Click to close the Technology Tree
en_US.LOC_META_55_BODY: Continue moving your Settler unit to the indicated location.
en_US.LOC_META_56_BODY: In choosing a location to settle a new city, it is important to look at the fertility of the surrounding land. Proximity to sources of [ICON_Food] Food, resources, and fresh water are all very important. For this tutorial we have already found an ideal location for you.
en_US.LOC_META_57_BODY: When your Settler unit is able, click the Found City button to create a new city here. This may require moving on to the next turn if your Settler is out of [ICON_Movement] Movement points.
en_US.LOC_META_58_BODY: To win a game of Civilization, as a player you need to defeat all other civilizations in the world. There are multiple ways to achieve this. You can conquer their cities militarily, bringing them into your civilization. You can also win technologically, or through cultural or religious dominance.
en_US.LOC_META_59_BODY: On the path to victory, there are fundamental strategies to assist you in building your civilization.[NEWLINE]---[NEWLINE]For this tutorial, we have provided four goals for you to achieve. Complete all four and you can complete the tutorial. However, in order to WIN the tutorial, you need to complete the fifth goal.
en_US.LOC_META_5_BODY: Click the Next Turn button to finish your turn.
en_US.LOC_META_5a_BODY: Civilization is a turn-based game where decisions are made and actions performed during a game turn, much like playing a board game with friends. Once all the other players have made their moves, a new turn will begin.
en_US.LOC_META_5b_BODY: Building items in your city takes time. The number of game turns it will take is indicated on each item in the menu.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]This is calculated based on the [ICON_Production] Production cost of the item versus the [ICON_Production] Production yield of the city. The higher the yield, the fewer turns it will take to build.
en_US.LOC_META_61_BODY: Congratulations![NEWLINE]---[NEWLINE]You have completed the fundamentals of growing and maintaining a civilization that will stand the test of time. You can finish the tutorial, or you can keep playing and win this game by eliminating the rival civ.
en_US.LOC_META_62_BODY: To win this game, you must conquer all the rival civilization’s city(s) with your military.[NEWLINE]---[NEWLINE]Good luck!
en_US.LOC_META_63_BODY: In this tutorial you are playing on a small map with a single rival civilization. A standard game of Civilization presents a larger map of the world, with several rival civilizations, all competing to win. The task is larger, but the goals remain the same.
en_US.LOC_META_64_BODY: Districts are specific areas of your city dedicated to providing a specific yield. Buildings can be constructed in districts to increase that yield while also providing other benefits for your city.
en_US.LOC_META_65_BODY: For example, you have unlocked the {DISTRICT_TYPE} district which is dedicated to providing {YIELD_TYPE} to your civilization. Constructing a {DISTRICT_BUILDING} building in this district increases the {YIELD_TYPE} yield for your civilization.
en_US.LOC_META_66_BODY: To zone a district, select it in your city’s production menu as you would a building or a unit. Some districts have rules of where they can be placed, but even more important is that districts can have an even greater benefit if placed in an optimal location.
en_US.LOC_META_67_BODY: When you are ready to zone a district, the game will assist you in choosing the best location. Sometimes you might not have a valid spot in your city to place a new district right away. The location may have to be cleared of obstructions, or all of your existing city plots may already have improvements.
en_US.LOC_META_68_BODY: Expanding the size of your city is one way to gain more locations for districts, as well as improvements.
en_US.LOC_META_69_BODY: Any research progress on a technology is not lost, so there are cases where changing your research focus is strategically valid. However, it is always better to have a completed technology rather than many incomplete ones.
en_US.LOC_META_6_BODY: Click the Choose Research button to open the Research Panel.
en_US.LOC_META_72_BODY: Any production progress on an item in the queue is not lost, so there are cases where changing your city’s production focus is strategically valid. However, it is often best to finish what you have started before starting something new.
en_US.LOC_META_73_BODY: In Civilization VI, you can get Eureka Moments that boost your technology research through in game achievements. This Eureka Moment was gained by discovering a natural wonder. Other achievements could be winning a battle with a specific unit or constructing a building. Achieving these greatly accelerates your technological progress.
en_US.LOC_META_74_BODY: You might have noticed that your Builder unit disappeared after using its last build ‘charge’. This is because all of its workforce has been expended. You will need to train more Builders as you progress through the game to improve the lands around your cities.
en_US.LOC_META_75_BODY: Scouts, unlike other military units, gain experience from exploring Tribal Villages. They can also gain experience from discovering natural wonders in the world.
en_US.LOC_META_76_BODY: Open the Production Chooser of your first city by clicking the production button on the City Banner.
en_US.LOC_META_77_BODY: In Civilization VI, there are many types of districts that can be built in your cities, each with a specific purpose.
en_US.LOC_META_78_BODY: By completing research on Writing, you are now able to construct a Campus district in your city.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]The Campus district is dedicated to increasing the amount of [ICON_Science] Science generated by the city that contains it.
en_US.LOC_META_79_BODY: Many districts in the game also get a bonus depending on where they are placed within the city. The Campus gets a bonus when built next to Mountains or Jungles.
en_US.LOC_META_7_BODY: Select the Mining technology from the menu to begin researching it.
en_US.LOC_META_7a_BODY: The Research Panel displays what technology your civilization is currently working toward. It is empty because you have not yet chosen a technology to research.
en_US.LOC_META_80_BODY: Click the Campus button in the Production Chooser to start building one in this city.
en_US.LOC_META_81_BODY: When placing a district, the map changes slightly to indicate ideal locations in which to build it.
en_US.LOC_META_82_BODY: This plot has Mountains on two of its edges, each providing +1 [ICON_Science] Science per turn. Placing the Campus here would be ideal.
en_US.LOC_META_83_BODY: Click this hex to begin building a Campus here.
en_US.LOC_META_84_BODY: Since you have finished the Writing technology, you now must choose what to research next. If you would like a suggestion, Animal Husbandry and Bronze Working are both good choices.
en_US.LOC_META_85_BODY: Animal Husbandry will allow you to build the Pasture and Camp improvements in your cities.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]Bronze Working will help you militarily by unlocking the Encampment district, as well as allow you to train Spearmen.
en_US.LOC_META_86_BODY: Some buildings can only be constructed in districts. The Library is a building exclusive to the Campus district. Since we have completed construction on the Campus, we are now able to build a Library on it.
en_US.LOC_META_87_BODY: Click the Choose Production button in the lower right to begin building a Library.
en_US.LOC_META_88_BODY: Congratulations!![NEWLINE]You have won your first game of Civilization.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]You are now ready to take on much larger challenges and objectives, explore new worlds, meet new civilizations for the first time, and achieve victory on your terms.
en_US.LOC_META_89_BODY: When engaged in a war with another civilization, it is best to have a sufficient number of combat units, both to defend your cities as well as fight abroad.
en_US.LOC_META_8_BODY: Since there are no more decisions to make this turn, click the Next Turn button to continue.
en_US.LOC_META_90_BODY: Sometimes it is necessary to suspend production on a building or district in order to train units to fight the war. To do this, simply change the current production task of the city to the combat unit you wish to create.
en_US.LOC_META_91_BODY: When you are satisfied with the size of your military, you can resume production on what was being built previously without losing the progress you made on it.
en_US.LOC_META_92_BODY: Engaging in diplomatic relations with other civilizations can be very lucrative. Of course, relations can also go sour. How you interact with other leaders is your choice. Just remember, in the path to victory, you cannot always be everyone’s friend.
en_US.LOC_META_93a_BODY: By accumulating [ICON_Culture] Culture, you have just unlocked Code of Laws, which contains your first government: Chiefdom.
en_US.LOC_META_93b_BODY: To access it, click the Government button.
en_US.LOC_META_94_BODY: There are many types of governments in Civilization VI. In addition to various benefits, each government has a number of slots in which you can enact policies.
en_US.LOC_META_95a_BODY: The first government available to you is Chiefdom. It has 2 available slots for policies. The first slot in Chiefdom is for Military policies. The second is for Economic policies.
en_US.LOC_META_96_BODY: To slot a policy, click and drag the policy from the right to the appropriate slot in your government on the left.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]Try that now by adding the Discipline policy to the Military slot, then add the Urban Planning policy to the Economic slot. Click the Confirm Policies button when you are done.
en_US.LOC_META_97_BODY: By enacting these policies, your military units will now get a +5 [ICON_Strength] Combat Strength bonus when fighting against Barbarians. Also, your cities receive +1 [ICON_Production] Production per turn, allowing them to train units and construct buildings faster than before.
en_US.LOC_META_98_BODY: Much in the same way you research new technologies by generating [ICON_Science] Science in your cities, you unlock civics by generating [ICON_Culture] Culture.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]You have already unlocked the Code of Laws civic which enabled you to establish your first government.
en_US.LOC_META_99a_BODY: Now you need to select a new civic to advance toward.
en_US.LOC_META_99b_BODY: Open the Civics Tree by clicking the Civics Tree button in the upper left corner of the screen.
en_US.LOC_META_9_BODY: Click on the Warrior unit to select it.

One source of [ICON_Amenities] Amenities are Luxury resources, such as this [ICON_Resource_Coffee] Coffee next to your [ICON_Capital] Capital. en_US.LOC_MOD_ALEXANDER_SCENARIO_DESCRIPTION: In this timed single-player scenario, you must rush to expand your empire to truly earn the title of "Alexander the Great." This scenario emphasizes combat, territorial expansion, and calculated use of the Great Generals who will fight by your side.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]To win, conquer every city on the map within a number of turns determined by your difficulty level:[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]Settler: 60 turns[NEWLINE]Warlord or Chieftain: 55 turns[NEWLINE]King or Prince: 50 turns[NEWLINE]Immortal or Emperor: 45 turns[NEWLINE]Deity: 37 turns
en_US.LOC_MOD_ALEXANDER_SCENARIO_TEASER: Can you conquer an empire worthy of Alexander the Great? Lasts no more than 60 Turns.
en_US.LOC_MOD_AUSTRALIA_SCENARIO_DESCRIPTION: In this 60 turn scenario, you race to explore Australia, find its natural resources, and use them to enrich your colony. This competitive economic scenario has no combat. It emphasizes exploration and territorial expansion to increase your Gold Per Turn net income, which is your score.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]Single-player: Each difficulty has a Gold Per Turn threshold. Exceed that number before the end of the game to win.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]Multiplayer: The player with the highest Gold Per Turn at end of the game is the winner.
en_US.LOC_MOD_AUSTRALIA_SCENARIO_TEASER: Which colony will make the most of Australia's natural riches?
en_US.LOC_MOD_INDONESIA_KHMER_SCENARIO_DESCRIP: The lands around the Indian Ocean flourish with many religions and many people. Heaven has chosen you to bring the light to all these lands. Is your faith up to the challenge? Can you convince the people of Southeast Asia to follow your religion?
en_US.LOC_MOD_INDONESIA_KHMER_SCENARIO_TEASER: Spread your faith across East Asia.
en_US.LOC_MOD_NUBIA_SCENARIO_DESCRIPTION: In this 125-turn scenario, you must expand your empire up and down the Nile River valley competing to become the people most blessed by the great god Amun.  Build 7 temples to his glory and victory is yours!
en_US.LOC_MOD_NUBIA_SCENARIO_TEASER: Can you become the dominant empire in the Nile River valley? Lasts no more than 125 Turns.
en_US.LOC_MOD_POLAND_SCENARIO_DESCRIPTION: In this 60 turn scenario, you stand at the crossroads of Europe, protecting the fertile Polish homelands from a constant barraging of invaders from all directions. Rally your Winged Hussars and face off against Teutonic Knights and Ottoman Turks as you grow your civilization.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]The player with best empire by standard scoring at end of the game is the winner.
en_US.LOC_MOD_POLAND_SCENARIO_TEASER: Fight alongside two other players to defend Poland from foreign invasions.
en_US.LOC_MOD_SCOUT_CAT_DESCRIPTION: Sometimes a player loves "Scout" the dog so much that they cannot stand to see Scout working so hard in the wild. So the obvious solution is to send in a clowder of cats so Scout can relax back at the village. Or, if you're a huge fan of felines, then this DLC is simply righting a wrong.
en_US.LOC_MOD_SCOUT_CAT_TEASER: Replaces the Scout's dog with a clowder of cats.
en_US.LOC_MOD_VIKINGSLANDMARKS_DESCRIPTION: Three new natural wonders and six new city states, including two that grant new tile improvements.
en_US.LOC_MOD_VIKINGSLANDMARKS_TEASER: Three new natural wonders and six new city states.
en_US.LOC_MOD_VIKINGS_SCENARIO_DESCRIPTION: Bring Europe under your rule as the mightiest Viking lord in this 60 turn scenario. Play as one of three unique Viking rulers from Denmark, Norway, or Sweden and pillage and raid your way through Europe. Launch a naval invasion of England, conquer Paris, or sail around Gibraltar and raid the Mediterranean Sea. [NEWLINE][NEWLINE] Back home, build a merchant empire as you accumulate trade routes with the most profitable cities that you can. And if you find yourself following a religion, spread the good word and generate [ICON_Faith] Faith for your people.
en_US.LOC_MOD_VIKINGS_SCENARIO_TEASER: As a viking king, can you amass the greatest wealth? Lasts 60 Turns.

en_US.LOC_PBC_NOTIFY_REMINDER_DESC: We recommend you enable notifications prior to starting a Play By Cloud match.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]You must have notifications configured to receive notifications outside of Sid Meier’s Civilization VI.
en_US.LOC_PBC_OVERVIEW_DESC: Play By Cloud is an asynchronous multiplayer format where all players take their turns on a common savegame, which is stored on a hosted server. This is a more modern version of “passing the savegame,” which was the ancient practice of sharing a floppy disk with a common save file between friends (if you are unfamiliar with the concept of a “floppy disk,” please ask a respected adult of venerable age).[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]A Play By Cloud game may last a long time (on the order of days or weeks) as each player takes his or her turn at a time that is convenient to them. You will receive notifications when it is your turn to play. You may see a Steam notification if Steam is active, or you may use the webhooks. Webhooks are a generic message format that the technically-inclined can integrate into other messaging services, email, or Internet of Things devices.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]In asynchronous multiplayer, it is considered courteous to take your turn at your earliest possible convenience to keep the game moving. In ancient times, players were morally obligated to protect the floppy disk from corruption, with unscrupulous players resorting to “losing” the savegame when in an untenable situation. Play By Cloud eliminates such rascally behavior.
en_US.LOC_PEDIA_BUILDINGS_PAGE_BUILDING_AIRPOR: Technically, an “airport” is any sort of location where airplanes, helicopters, blimps, or other aircraft can take off and land. However, in common usage an airport is a complex for commercial passenger aircraft, consisting of runways, control towers, hangers, terminals, emergency facilities and even parking structures. Man’s tendency to be in a hurry has made airports an inherent part of every city landscape (although most commercial airports are now located well away from the city, given the noise and pollution). Prior to 1930, most airports were small airfields or aerodromes, with runways of less than 2000 feet. In 1939 busy La Guardia in New York City handled nearly a quarter million passengers a month; the most recent statistics for airport passenger traffic list Hartsfield-Jackson in Atlanta as the world’s busiest, with over 92 million passing through it in 2011.
en_US.LOC_PEDIA_BUILDINGS_PAGE_BUILDING_AMPHIT: When bread and circuses didn’t keep the masses happy, there was always the theater to distract them. An amphitheater is an outdoor arena (modern usage of the term is rather lax) that serves as a venue for performances, sporting events and public speeches. Although there had certainly been public spectacles in various places before, these tended to be staged ad hoc. But when the Greeks began writing plays around 532 BC, they built small, open-air structures (called theatrons) in which to perform these; the Romans, always looking to build bigger and better, created the amphitheater. The Romans built them all over their conquered lands, for every frontier outpost wanted to be civilized. The practice spread outward from the empire to other places, for amphitheaters were great places to stage plays, gladiatorial and Olympic Games, religious spectacles, executions, political debates, concerts, and all manner of other entertainments.
en_US.LOC_PEDIA_BUILDINGS_PAGE_BUILDING_ARENA_: An indoor amphitheater … an “arena,” from the Latin harena, a fine sand that was very good at absorbing blood in colosseums across the Roman Empire. These days, that has been forgotten by all those who go to arenas to watch sporting events, concerts, and other performances (such as political speeches). The most distinguishing feature of an arena is that the performance area is the lowest point in the main space, with seating for spectators banked up around it. Since the ancients had some difficulty roofing over large areas, it is unknown what might be termed civilization’s first indoor arena, although the famed Colosseum had retractable awnings to cover the spectators’ area. Currently the largest arena in the world is the Philippine Arena in Bocaue, seating about 55 thousand. But likely the best known is Madison Square Garden in Manhattan, fourth of that name, the first opening in 1879 AD under lease to P.T. Barnum. The current Garden, seating between 18 and 20 thousand depending on event, opened in 1968 and has been home to heartache and history ever since.
en_US.LOC_PEDIA_BUILDINGS_PAGE_BUILDING_ARMORY: An armory (or arsenal, the terms tend to get mixed although there are some significant differences) is the place where arms and armor are manufactured, repaired and/or stored when not being used to kill other people – i.e., during peacetime. Unless planning on facing the enemy, soldiers usually do not carry their weapons and armor about with them (especially if their weapons were lances and their armor plate). The first armories date back to the first professional armies, those of Sumer and Akkad. Every standing army since has had armories, perhaps as simple as a well-guarded (wouldn’t do to let the commoners get hold of any weapons) warehouse or as elaborate as a production facility making muskets. Given that it didn’t make sense to have the weapons on the other side of the city from the troops, the armory was usually near the barracks. Armories have even shaped the course of civilization, for a variety of reasons: the Tower of London, Harper’s Ferry, the Kremlin Armory, Springfield Armory, the Zeughaus in Berlin, and so forth.
en_US.LOC_PEDIA_BUILDINGS_PAGE_BUILDING_BANK_C: Although there had been money-lenders and treasuries before (money, after all, greases the wheels of civilization), banking begins in early Renaissance Italy, in the rich cities of the north such as Genoa, Venice, Florence, Siena and Lucca. During the 14th Century, already wealthy, avaricious families – the Bardi, de Medici, Peruzzi, Cerchi, Gondi and others – not only dominated the commercial banking in their home city-states but established branches across Europe. The oldest bank still in operation is the Monte dei Paschi in Siena, operating continuously since 1472 AD. Banking spread across the Holy Roman Empire and the northern European nations by 1600, and the Europeans took the practice with them when they set out to colonize the world. Although the details have changed dramatically with technology, the basics of banking profits remain the same: checking and savings fees, loans and credit cards, currency exchanges, fund management, and so forth.
en_US.LOC_PEDIA_BUILDINGS_PAGE_BUILDING_BARRAC: Militiamen had homes, had jobs, and fed and clothed themselves, waging war only when called out by the government; professional soldiers had no homes, war was their occupation, and they got their victuals and spiffy uniforms from the government. Once writing was invented, professional armies were possible (along with most everything else, including kings and civilizations). Since they didn’t have homes as such, the barracks housed them … usually near the center of town so the soldiers could react to any threat, external or internal. Effectively, the barracks were permanent camps, with such amenities as training grounds, bath rooms, medical facilities, mess halls and gymnasia added. Often these barracks were at least minimally fortified, just in case of trouble. Be it ever so humble, home is where the heart is … in this case, war.
en_US.LOC_PEDIA_BUILDINGS_PAGE_BUILDING_BROADC: It wasn’t long after commercial radio began being broadcast that the first “broadcast center” was built: Broadcasting House, home of the British Broadcasting Corporation (the world’s oldest and largest), in 1932 AD. A “broadcasting center” is a complex (studios, sound booths, antennae, and lots of esoteric electrical equipment) for sending out radio and television waves to home receivers, thus keeping folk passively entertained for hours at a time. The BBC was chartered in 1922 as a government-supported operation to supply edifying entertainment and information to the people of Great Britain. Soon after, a number of Commonwealth nations took the same approach, as did a handful of other countries. In the American model, private broadcasting corporations provided competitive programming, funded by the sale of advertising time to “sponsors.” By 1928, the United States had three national networks (two owned by NBC). These competing (for audience numbers, which translate to advertising revenues) networks each built their own broadcasting center(s) to feed the electronic wasteland.
en_US.LOC_PEDIA_BUILDINGS_PAGE_BUILDING_CASTLE: From the Latin castellum, a castle is designed to protect the important people (and maybe those who serve them) from their enemies. Surrounded sometimes by moats and mottes, often with palisades and baileys and enceinte, usually with a central keep for when things really went wrong, the great castles were the last refuge during times of troubles. From the walls and towers the dedicated defenders could hurl death down upon the attackers … who, if they were smart, simply laid siege to the pile until those inside starved and sensibly surrendered. Historians are not quite sure (hardly surprising) when castles as such arose, but most attribute the development to an evolution of the walls around lordly homes to protect such from the likes of the Magyars, Muslims and Vikings in the 9th and 10th centuries AD. Proven Roman engineering techniques were adapted to make these outposts of civilization as nigh impregnable as possible. And, in time, royalty decided they might need some in their cities as well, for when the peasants started revolting. Worked well enough, until those peasants had gunpowder.
en_US.LOC_PEDIA_BUILDINGS_PAGE_BUILDING_CATHED: Once there were Catholic churches at every crossroads in Italy, some bishops decided they needed something grander to serve as the seat of each diocese or episcopate. Thus, the cathedral – from the Latin cathedra meaning “seat” or “chair.” The concept of cathedrals begins in 313 AD, when the emperor Constantine adopted Christianity; with that, Christianity went from being a minor faith to the religion of Rome, and the bishops agreed, more or less willingly, to take on the duties and dignity of magistrates across the empire. Since the old Roman magistrates had presided from a throne housed in a highly decorated hall (basilica), it wasn’t long before the bishops (who had never before been seated while presiding over their flock) began building cathedrals, massive edifices designed to impress the peasants with the glory of God. With money, materials and labor “donated” by the faithful peasants, these often took a lifetime to build … but are among some of the most impressive structures in all civilization. The first cathedral was that at Aquileia (c. 319) and they haven’t stopped building them yet.
en_US.LOC_PEDIA_BUILDINGS_PAGE_BUILDING_DAR_E_: First seen around the Ninth Century BCE, the first Zoroastrian structures called 'Dar-e Mehr' are linked to the concept of 'Atar' ("holy fire"). The fire and clean water at the center of the Dar-e Mehr aren't worshipped, but instead a means to gain ritual purity.

A temple would be named depending on the type of fire housed within, with the holiest being the "Fire of Victory," or 'Atash Behram,' requiring 32 priests and a year of burning fires from 16 sanctified sources to be considered consecrated.

These temples, usually constructed on a hill or higher location, contain ritualized flames housed in a chamber called the atashgah. However, if you're a non-believer, don't expect to see the atashgah or the flame inside: tradition dictates that only the faithful be allowed to view the holy fire.
en_US.LOC_PEDIA_BUILDINGS_PAGE_BUILDING_ELECTR: With the advent of consumer electronics, the market for all manner of gizmos and gadgets for entertainment, communication and wasting time exploded in the late 20th Century. The Consumer Electronics Association estimated that sales of electronics for personal use – from computers to MP3 players, calculators to digital cameras, and so forth – exceeded 150 billion dollars in 2007 AD. To feed this postmodern addiction, semi-skilled laborers working in sprawling electronics factories assemble standardized parts into an ever-increasing flood of new products. Leading the way in this tidal wave is Japan, with the largest electronics industry in the world, although both South Korea and China are increasingly competitive. The first “modern” electronics factory was built by Sony, founded in 1946 AD. In the 1950s, Japanese engineers pioneered commercial applications for the transistor and in the 1970s and 1980s for the semi-conductor. Japanese innovations in miniaturization and in standardizing electronics manufacturing have kept their factories the most profitable in the most competitive field in consumerism ever seen.
en_US.LOC_PEDIA_BUILDINGS_PAGE_BUILDING_FACTOR: The Industrial Revolution came upon civilization, and all those things once made by hand are soon made in factories… and in great quantities. The workshops, where master craftsmen proudly made things by hand, gave way to the assembly line and the mass production of standardized products. The Englishman Richard Arkwright is credited with creating the prototype for the modern factory; in 1769 he patented the “water frame,” a water-powered spinning device, and built Cromford Mill in Derbyshire. In the process, he replaced skilled workers (on spinning wheels) with unskilled migrants who could produce more yarn quicker (albeit of poorer quality); in effect, Arkwright made workers a replaceable commodity in his plant. Soon enough, others copied the formula, and it was applied to other industries as technology brought steam, and then electricity, to the workshops. The final step in the industrialization of the workplace: Henry Ford revolutionized factory production with the first assembly line in 1913, capable of producing a Model T Ford using interchangeable parts in 93 minutes.
en_US.LOC_PEDIA_BUILDINGS_PAGE_BUILDING_FILM_S: The “Black Maria,” a tarpaper-covered shack in West Orange, New Jersey, built by Thomas Edison in 1893 AD, might generously be termed the first “movie studio”; there Edison used film to capture the antics of vaudeville and theater actors to show to the public in penny arcades, unused theaters, and fairground tents. In 1909, Edwin Thanhouser leased an old skating rink and made commercial films, some 1086 between 1910 and 1917. Meanwhile in Europe, studios such as Pathé (France), Münchner Lichtspielkunst AG (Bavaria). Mosfilm (Russia) and Ealing Studios (UK) were being founded. But, for unexplained reasons, a number of studios sprouted up in and around Los Angeles (the best explanation being that natural sunlight was the best for the crude movie cameras of the time), the first being Nestor Studios in 1911. By 1920, there were a dozen in operation in the suburb of Hollywood cranking out film by the mile to feed civilization’s latest escapist addiction. Although film studios are largely passé (most production taking place “on location”), some remain in operation in odd corners of the globe.
en_US.LOC_PEDIA_BUILDINGS_PAGE_BUILDING_GRANAR: Once farming really took off, some place was needed to put that surplus grain to keep it safe from rats, insects, and other humans. The oldest granaries yet uncovered date back to the pre-pottery Neolithic period in the Jordan Valley, c. 9500 BC. In the Indus Valley, the oldest date to 6000 BC, and the Egyptians were storing surplus grain in “silo” pits as a hedge against poor harvests by this time as well. In East Asia, the Yangshao in China were building elevated granaries along the Yellow River around 5000 BC, and eventually the Koreans (c. 1000 BC) and the Japanese (c. 800 BC) figured it out as well. In modern times, granaries – like all else – have gotten larger, automated, and more complex; the rich farmlands of the United States and Russia, especially, are dotted with huge silos and grain elevators to help feed the teeming masses of civilization.
en_US.LOC_PEDIA_BUILDINGS_PAGE_BUILDING_GURDWA: A gurdwara (meaning “the gateway to the guru”) is a Sikh temple, although those of all faiths are welcomed to worship in their own way there. The gurdwara traditionally has a great hall (the Darbar Sahib) where the Guru Granth Sahib is displayed and a Langar where visitors can partake of the free food offered by the Sikh community. The egalitarian complex may also have a nursery, library, hospital and/or classrooms. The very first Sikh guru, Nanak Dev Ji, built the very first gurdwara in 1521 AD on the banks of the Ravi River of the Punjab … so legend has it. The first gurdwaras were the places for the faithful to gather to hear the current guru speak and to sing hymns to Waheguru (loosely, “God”). It was the sixth Sikh guru who finally gave such places the name “gurdwara.” Since meditation and the study of the scriptures are central to Sikhism, the gurdwara is vital to the “proper” moral and spiritual development of a Sikh.
en_US.LOC_PEDIA_BUILDINGS_PAGE_BUILDING_HANGAR: Ships need docks; airplanes need hangars. It was quickly discovered that the early heavier-than-air craft tended to need protection from the weather, repair, and constant maintenance, and all of this was best done inside cavernous structures made of wood and fabric (now, virtually all hangars are made of metal and/or concrete). The bigger the aircraft, the bigger the hangar necessary; XXL hangars (more than 120 meters across) are used to house the world’s largest aircraft: the Airbus A380, Antonov 225, and Boeing 747. But the largest hangars in civilization were those built for the zeppelins and dirigibles, such as the U.S. Navy’s Hangar 1 located at Lakehurst (the site of the Hindenburg disaster). From the S to the XXL, hangars are vital to the operations of military airfields and civilian airports in this fast-paced era (thus, hangars are prime targets in any modern war).
en_US.LOC_PEDIA_BUILDINGS_PAGE_BUILDING_LIBRAR: Once literacy fastened on civilization, it was inevitable that reading materials (books, periodicals, maps, newspapers, scrolls, tablets, documents of all sorts) should be gathered in one place – a library. The first libraries, those of Sumer dating back to approximately 2600 BC, were archives of clay tablets covered in cuneiform script. Over 30 thousand clay tablets have been unearthed in the Library of Ashurbanipal in Nineveh, including the Epic of Gilgamesh. The Library of Alexandria was the greatest and most significant library in the classical world, but it was burned – a fate most great libraries suffer, it seems. While Europe plunged into a Dark Age, libraries flourished under the Muslim Arabs, whose development of papermaking helped considerably in their acquisition of texts from the known world. Although many of these historical libraries were open to all, the foundation of free, public libraries came with the British Public Libraries Act of 1850, a boon to the literate (about 76% in 1870) no matter their low birth.
en_US.LOC_PEDIA_BUILDINGS_PAGE_BUILDING_LIGHTH: The sea is a dangerous place, filled with shoals, shallows, reefs, and rocks just waiting to bring the unwary ship to grief. And the weary crew might have a difficult time finding safe harbor. So, in antiquity, not long after men began sailing, signal fires were lit to guide the ship away from danger to port; since such signal fires would be even more visible if elevated, “lighthouses” began to be built by the first seafaring civilizations on promontories. The most famous of the ancient ones: the Pharos at Alexandria, of course, which guided ships into what was once the busiest seaport in the world. For two thousand years since, lighthouses were built wherever there was a need for sailors not to drown and cargos not to be lost. Stone, wood, and brick have given way to steel and concrete construction, and fire has given way to arc lamps, but the principle remains the same.
en_US.LOC_PEDIA_BUILDINGS_PAGE_BUILDING_MADRAS: A madrasa (madrasah in Arabic or medrese in Turkish) is a secular institution of education, although often with a religious component. Madrasas would specialize in medicine, law, science, philosophy, religion or the education of women. Others also taught logic, world history, foreign languages, mathematics, art, and comparative literature. The first madrasa, the Gama'at al-Qarawiyyn, was established in 859 AD by Fatimah al-Fihri, the daughter of a wealthy merchant. During the rule of the Fatimid, Ayyubid, and Mamluk dynasties, the practice of sponsoring madrasas by the ruling, wealthy elite spread across Egypt and the Middle East. The first Ottoman madrasa was founded in 1331 in Iznik, and followed the traditions of Sunni Islam. The madrasas of the Turks and Arabs would, as Europe stumbled through the Dark Ages, keep the best of Classical knowledge alive, and build on it with their own inventions.
en_US.LOC_PEDIA_BUILDINGS_PAGE_BUILDING_MARKET: Whether called a souk (Arabic), bazaar (Persian), mercado (Spanish) or palengke (Filipino), markets have been around since farmers had surpluses and tradesmen had wares to sell to townsfolk. While primitive markets may have operated on a barter system, it was the coming of writing and coinage that made markets profitable and, indeed, indispensable to civilization. Markets were located in towns, both transport hubs and centers of consumption, even when the latter were off the beaten track. Marketplaces in Thebes, Babylon, Athens, Rome, Bangkok, Marrakech, London, Delhi, in all places and all times, offered the exotic, innovative and everyday for sale. Their shape and style may differ dramatically – floating markets, indoor markets, street markets, night markets, market squares, ad infinitum – but the intent is the same: to make a profit for the stallholders.
en_US.LOC_PEDIA_BUILDINGS_PAGE_BUILDING_MBANZA: Mbanza is Kongolese for “city,” or in some cases simply “settlement.” By the time the Portuguese arrived in central Africa, M’banza Kongo was already a large city, rich from trade and craft manufacturing, but most of the population lived in the valleys that surrounded it in residential neighborhoods – perhaps as many as 100 thousand people. While these small towns might have a market and a workshop, the important things – churches, palace, schools, clinics, tax offices – were located in the hilltop capital. They were linked to M’banza Kongo by several roads up the slopes, and these were quite crowded at times such as feast and tax days. All this in 1648 AD according to the visitor Francesco da Roma. So not only did the Kongolese give civilization suburbia but also “rush hour.”
en_US.LOC_PEDIA_BUILDINGS_PAGE_BUILDING_MEETIN: In opposition to the magnificent cathedrals and churches of the Catholic Church, the Protestants thought worship should be serious and undistracted by art. Hence some Congregationalists worshipped in meeting houses - plain, unadorned buildings built from local resources (usually wood and stone). In the New World, the social and cultural center for most of the Protestant colonies was the meeting house, which served as both a place of worship and of public discourse for the settlers. For many early Quaker, Mennonite, Unitarian, Puritan, Baptist and other pious types, the meeting house also served as the de facto town hall, where political debates, votes and decisions were conducted. All along the Atlantic coast colonies, the first public building to go up was typically the meeting house. Once the separation of church and state became a widespread principal in the new United States, those meeting houses were all converted into town halls.
en_US.LOC_PEDIA_BUILDINGS_PAGE_BUILDING_MILITA: If a civilization is to have a professional army, then it needs professionals to run it. (It helps, but certainly doesn’t guarantee, that that expensive army won’t get wasted anyway.) A military academy is an institution of “higher” learning in the “art” of war, dedicated to training officers. The first military academies were established in the early 1700s in Europe (the oldest, the Royal Military Academy at Woolwich in 1720 AD) to train officers in the “technical” branches of the army, such as the engineers and the artillery. In France, the École Royale Militaire was founded in 1751, the first to offer a general military education. Within a generation, Prussia, Russia, Austria, Sweden and most of the lesser European states had military academies turning out army officers. And why not start teaching boys the ways of war as well, so private boarding schools for pre-collegiate cadets were established in the United Kingdom (such as Welbeck College), France (Saint-Cyr for instance), the United States (Valley Forge Military Academy and others), Russia (the Suvorov Military Schools) and elsewhere.
en_US.LOC_PEDIA_BUILDINGS_PAGE_BUILDING_MONUME: Since humans seem to be a forgetful sort – or perhaps just egotistical – they put up monuments to commemorate all kinds of things – “important” people, events, military victories, deities, or even fictional characters (such as that to Peter Pan in Kensington Gardens). They seem to especially like to stick them up in the middle of cities, so everyone has to see them and walk or drive around them. Monuments come in all shapes and sizes, beautiful and horrid. Triumphal arches, columns, obelisks, memorials and cenotaphs can be found in almost any large urban metropolis, supposedly infusing the inhabitants with civic and national pride. Or, as is usually the case, serving as nesting places for pigeons and recognizable backgrounds for tourist snapshots.
en_US.LOC_PEDIA_BUILDINGS_PAGE_BUILDING_MOSQUE: There are strict requirements and standards in Islamic fiqh for a building to be a mosque, and those places of worship that do not meet those are merely musallas (“gathering houses”). Under Sharia law, once a mosque is formally designated as a holy place, it remains that until the Day of Judgment (Yawm ad-Din). The oldest and largest mosque in the world, the Masjid al-Haram, was built in the city of Mecca around 638 AD; it encompasses the holy site of the Kaaba, the most sacred of all locations in Islam. The Prophet himself established other mosques, notably that at Medina. From there, mosques – with their distinctive domes, minarets and prayer halls overseen by an imam – were carried by the swords of the faithful across Arabia, the Middle East and North Africa during the 7th Century. The first mosque built in the Far East – that at Xi’an – reportedly dates to the mid-8th Century. A site of prayer, charity and learning, the mosque is the physical heart of Islamic civilization.
en_US.LOC_PEDIA_BUILDINGS_PAGE_BUILDING_MUSEUM: Humans generate lots of junk. They are also fascinated with old junk, and so created museums. A museum is a building designed to hold civilization’s most treasured possessions for public viewing. There are museums that contain collections of art, and there are the museums which display fossils, items of historical interest, or pop culture curiosities. There are also museums that house costumes, jewels, weapons, gadgets, or virtually anything else which might be of interest to the humans filing through their halls. The oldest known collection of curiosities put on display was that of Ennigaldi-Nanna’s Museum, c. 530 BC, with enough traffic to warrant labels for the items (a clue to archaeologists that the ruin was a museum). But the whole idea of such collections for public edification really took off during the Enlightenment, with the Royal Armories in the Tower of London, the Musée des Beaux-Arts et d’Archeologie in Besancon, and the Kunstkamera in St. Petersburg being founded. These and other museums are now almost as historic as the junk they display.

Art museums (or art galleries) are public spaces - paid for by the public, usually in the form of taxes – to house artwork meant to edify and uplift the masses. The art objects may take many forms: paintings, sketches, sculptures, ceramics, metalwork, prints, and now even video. Perhaps the first such effort at bringing high culture to the public took place in 1671 AD, the Amerbach-Cabinet in Basel (now the Kunstmuseum). But the whole idea of such collections for public edification really took off during the Renaissance, with the likes of the Capitoline, Vatican, and Uffizi galleries established. The 1700s saw another wave of iconic collections open: the Hermitage, the Prado, the Louvre, and the first American museum, the Charleston Museum, in 1773. The Louvre was established in 1793, soon after the French Revolution when the royal collection of art was declared the property of the people, beginning the trend of removing art from the grasp of the wealthy and putting it on tasteful display for the public to gawk at.
en_US.LOC_PEDIA_BUILDINGS_PAGE_BUILDING_PAGODA: Technically, a “pagoda” is a building style – a tiered tower with overhanging eaves – rather than a building, but for the unenlightened it has come to be the generic term for religious structures in the Far East, mostly Buddhist but also Taoist, Shinto and Confucian. The origin of the pagoda structure can be traced to the stupas of 3rd Century BC Nepal. From there, the architectural style spread across China and East Asia, where the Buddhists adopted it for their buildings housing sacred relics and texts. For Buddhist missionaries, pilgrims and priests, these pagodas became the centers of their faith on Earth with images of Gautama Buddha prominent and plentiful. The building materials and decoration, from unadorned to ornate, varied widely from region to region and faith to faith. But pagodas traditionally have an odd number of levels, the notable exception being the 163-foot “pagoda folly” erected by Sir William Chambers at Kew Gardens in London in 1762 and thought clever by the English.
en_US.LOC_PEDIA_BUILDINGS_PAGE_BUILDING_PALACE: As soon as some chieftain managed to become a king, he (or she) began to have delusions of grandeur; living in a hut like everyone else just wouldn’t do. A palace is the residence of a civilization's ruler. The term is somewhat anachronistic, since all sorts of things are called “palaces” nowadays, even gambling casinos. Currently most rulers live in ornate buildings called something like “the White House” or “Government House,” but the effect is the same. Palaces (and their modern equivalents) are designed to do three things: to provide the ruler with access to the people and communications necessary to rule, to defend the leader from attack, and to impress upon subjects and foreign visitors the leader's importance and staggering hubris.
en_US.LOC_PEDIA_BUILDINGS_PAGE_BUILDING_POWER_: The sole purpose of a power plant (or power station, generating plant, or power house) – be it hydro, nuclear, solar, fossil fuel-fired, tidal or other – is to feed the voracious appetite for electricity that civilization has developed over the past 160 years. Whatever the form, the principle is the same: convert one type of energy into another so that humans can enjoy their comforts. The first power plant was designed and built by Baron William Armstrong in 1868 AD (when scientists were still playing around with electricity in labs) in Cragside; water from a lake was used to turn the dynamos, and the resulting electricity powered lights, heating, hot water heaters, an elevator, and other odd devices in his properties nearby. In January 1882 the first public power plant came online in London, and in September the Pearl Street Station began operations in New York City supplying electricity to lower Manhattan. Although the Pearl Street Station burned down in 1890, it was too late – people were hooked on electric lights, and now over 7300 power plants operate in the United States alone.
en_US.LOC_PEDIA_BUILDINGS_PAGE_BUILDING_RESEAR: A research lab is an institute devoted to the advanced study of a subject, which might be medicine, physics, chemistry, robotics, clean energy, or new products for TV infomercials. Such labs may be publicly funded or run by wealthy corporations looking for profits; research labs may be attached to universities or they may be independent of academic boundaries and ethics. It is pretty clear that “efficient” research labs are the future of research in every discipline. As civilization’s understanding of the world has advanced, the days of the dedicated scientist working alone in his or her basement and shouting “Eureka!” have all but passed. Whatever understanding we may gain of the natural world, whatever new tech toy may grab our attention, whatever improvement of our daily life may come, whatever horrors may be unleashed, it will likely come out of a research laboratory, whether large (CERN’s Large Hadron Collider) or small (computer simulation modelling).
en_US.LOC_PEDIA_BUILDINGS_PAGE_BUILDING_SEAPOR: The sites of ancient ports were selected to optimize access to land or river routes, protect the anchored shipping, and maximize harbor fees – Guangzhou in Qin China, Piraeus for Athens, Canopus and Alexandria in Egypt, Lothal for the Harappan, Rome's Ostia Antica.
